title: Human Sacrifice in Iron Age Britain: The Ones Thrown Into Storage Pits Were Outsiders
dek: The five sets of human bones from the storage pits at the Duropolis site in Dorset are not like the bog bodies: these were not venerated elites but malnourished, hard-labouring outsiders with their wrists bound.
why: Archaeologist Miles Russell uses first-hand material from 17 years of excavation to strip ‘human sacrifice’ back from Roman propaganda to testable skeletal evidence. Dense with information, but it asks for a little patience.
who: Listeners interested in Iron Age archaeology, the credibility of Roman texts, prehistoric religion and ritual violence; anyone who wants to see how archaeology reasons from bones back to social structure.
skip: The first 2 minutes of small talk and T-shirt chatter can be skipped; fast-forward straight through the Gone Medieval ad in the middle.

points.h: Romans condemned human sacrifice while watching gladiators
points.body: Roman writers described the Britons as barbarians who practised human sacrifice, ate people and married their sisters, and Caesar's wicker man is part of that propaganda. But Miles points to a double standard: the Romans thought killing people to please the gods was wrong, yet they crucified thousands and let gladiators be torn apart by wild beasts in the arena as public entertainment. The difference is not whether you kill but who you kill for — killing for a god is barbaric, killing for an audience is enforcement. That cultural blind spot is the starting point for understanding every Roman account of human sacrifice.

points.h: Ninety-nine per cent of Britons never entered the burial record
points.body: To judge whether there was human sacrifice, you first need bones. But across most of late Iron Age Britain there is almost no skeletal remains at all; Miles estimates that roughly 99% of the population never appears in the archaeological record — perhaps cremated, perhaps left exposed, perhaps thrown into rivers or bogs. Only a few regions, such as Dorset and East Yorkshire, have large inhumation cemeteries. That means ‘no evidence of human sacrifice found’ and ‘no human sacrifice’ are two different things: the silence of archaeology is a sampling problem, not a conclusion.

points.h: Lindow Man was killed by four methods stacked together
points.body: Lindow Man is England's most famous bog body, his upper body beautifully preserved: neatly trimmed nails, groomed hair, good nutrition, suggesting he was well treated in life. But he died what Miles calls a ‘fourfold death’ — a blow to the head that fractured his skull, his throat cut, strangulation, and finally being placed face down in the bog possibly still alive, with water found in his lungs. The cut throat plus strangulation was meant to make the blood spurt further, a theatrical execution. In his stomach were an oatcake and mistletoe, the latter possibly used to induce hallucinations or dull pain, bringing him closer to the gods.

points.h: The bones in the storage pits were discarded, not buried
points.body: At hillforts such as Danebury, human bones often turn up at the bottom of disused cylindrical storage pits, mixed in with animal bone. Some are just a skull with mandible and a few cervical vertebrae, indicating death by decapitation rather than the head being taken after death; others were thrown in whole. Miles stresses that this is not a formal burial, with relatives laying the body down in tears and grave goods, but ‘someone being disposed of in a very dramatic, violent way’. Yet the bones in the pits could also be heroes who fell in battle, so bones alone cannot distinguish execution, death in combat and human sacrifice — the key is whether the burial context is anomalous.

points.h: Winterbourne Woman had her throat cut and was thrown onto a bone platform
points.body: In 2010 an adult female was found at the bottom of a storage pit at Duropolis, face down on a layer of long-weathered horse, cattle and pig bone forming a platform. Her skeleton shows a heavy blow to the chest a few weeks before death, with a cracked rib healing, plus head injuries, and the fatal wound: a deep cut on the cervical vertebrae — someone had opened her carotid artery from behind with a blade. DNA shows she was unrelated to any of the families in the cemetery, isotopes show she did not grow up on the chalk, and severe compression of her vertebrae indicates long-term load-bearing. Miles concludes she was probably a slave or a prisoner of war, an ‘outsider’, and that is why she was chosen.

points.h: This society was matrilocal, so they did not kill their own
points.body: DNA research by Laura Cassidy and University College Dublin shows that the women of Duropolis stayed on the same land for generations while the men came from further away and were more weakly linked to the women; women had more grave goods, and land may have passed down the female line. This explains a brutal logic: the people thrown into the pits were not local women, because they were the landholders and possibly the spiritual leaders who conducted the rites. Miles says that looking at their roundhouses and settlements you would think it a utopia, but seeing the human sacrifice makes you realise their attitude to life was completely different from ours.

points.h: At the pit edge the archaeologist sees a crime scene
points.body: Duropolis has produced five probable human sacrifices: four clearly thrown in, limbs scattered; one face down but with the legs tucked under the body, possibly having been bound. One adult male had one leg braced against the pit wall and his foot in the topmost layer — the archaeologists dug the foot first and then the man, so they could reconstruct clearly how he was thrown in from the pit mouth after being killed. Miles says that normally you excavate people who were buried, but this time ‘you are actually dealing with a murder victim’: you can see the victim, the manner of death and the place of death, but you will never find the murderer.

points.h: The bog holds elites, the pits hold the bottom of society
points.body: Miles proposes a stratified theory: bog bodies such as Lindow Man and the Irish examples have clean nails and no calluses on their hands, did no heavy manual labour, and may have been priests or ruling elites — some scholars even think kings, with power traded against ‘ultimately sacrificing yourself’. The people in the Duropolis storage pits did heavy work, were malnourished and had their wrists bound; they belonged to the bottom of society and were seen as more expendable. Both are human lives given up, but the bog is ‘claimed by the gods’ while the storage pit is merely ‘thrown in with the rubbish’.

terms.def: An ancient human body preserved in acidic, oxygen-poor peat bog, where skin, internal organs and even stomach contents can survive.
A transitional zone between two worlds, such as rivers and bogs, believed to be inhabited by gods and to offer passage to another world.
A social form in which men move after marriage to live with the woman's family, with land and status often passing down the female line.
Inferring an individual's place of upbringing, diet and migration from the isotope ratios in bones and teeth.
A fungus parasitic on grain that can cause hallucinations, speculated by some scholars to have been used before sacrifice to alter the sacrificial victim's state of consciousness.
